main_dishes.name: Sambar
main_dishes.description: Palakkad-style sambar with freshly ground masala — tangy, aromatic, and hearty. The hallmark is the home-ground paste of roasted coriander seeds, chana dal, red chilies, and coconut.

ingredients.name: Dry red chilies
ingredients.note: for grinding — adjust to taste, this is house-style spice level

steps.instruction: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric and water until soft (3-4 whistles). Mash well and set aside.

Dry roast coriander seeds (1.5 tbsp), chana dal (2 tsp), fenugreek seeds (1/4 tsp), and dry red chilies (13) in a pan on medium heat until fragrant and chana dal turns golden — about 3-4 minutes. Let cool.
Add roasted spices and grated coconut (3/4 cup) to a mixer/grinder. Grind to a SMOOTH paste with a little water. This is the sambar masala — the soul of this sambar.
Soak tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water for 15 minutes. Squeeze and extract thick tamarind water. Discard pulp.
In a heavy-bottomed pot, bring tamarind extract to a boil with salt and turmeric. Let it boil for 8-10 minutes until the raw tamarind smell goes away completely.
Add drumstick pieces, tomato quarters, and halved shallots to the boiling tamarind water. Cook until drumstick is tender (10-12 minutes).
Add the ground sambar masala paste. Stir well and simmer for 5-7 minutes until the raw smell of the paste disappears and the sambar thickens slightly.
Add the mashed toor dal. Mix well. Adjust consistency with water — should be neither too thick nor too thin. Add jaggery (small piece) if desired. Simmer 5 minutes.
Temper: Heat coconut oil/ghee in a small pan. Add mustard seeds — when they splutter, add curry leaves and a pinch of asafoetida. Pour into the sambar.
Cover and let rest for 5 minutes before serving. Sambar tastes better after resting.

main_dishes.critical_notes: The key to this sambar is the freshly ground masala — roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 2 tsp chana dal, 13 red chilies, 3/4 cup coconut and grind SMOOTH. The 13 chilies are house-style — it should be spicy but balanced by the tamarind and jaggery. Boil the tamarind extract long enough that the raw smell completely goes.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Before adding the ground masala paste (step 7), set aside 1-2 ladles of cooked dal + vegetable broth for the kid. This gives her a mild dal-vegetable mix without the spice. Or make a very small batch of sambar with only 3-4 chilies in the paste.

main_dishes.name: Avial
main_dishes.description: Classic Kerala/Palakkad-style avial — a medley of vegetables in a coconut-cumin-yogurt sauce, finished with raw coconut oil and curry leaves. A temple-festival staple.

steps.instruction: Cut all vegetables into uniform finger-sized pieces (about 2-3 inches long, 1/2 inch thick). Keep harder vegetables (drumstick, raw banana, yam) separate from softer ones (beans, carrot, ash gourd).
Grind coconut (1 cup), cumin seeds (1 tsp), and green chilies (4-5) to a COARSE paste — not too smooth, should have some texture. Use minimal water.
Cook the harder vegetables (drumstick, raw banana, yam) first in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan with 1/2 cup water, turmeric, and salt. Cover and cook for 8-10 minutes until half done.
Add the softer vegetables (beans, carrot, ash gourd). Add a splash more water if needed. Cover and cook for another 7-8 minutes until all vegetables are just tender — NOT mushy.
Add the ground coconut-cumin paste. Gently fold into the vegetables — do NOT stir vigorously as vegetables should hold their shape. Simmer for 4-5 minutes.
Remove from heat. Let it cool for 2 minutes, then add the whisked curd. Gently fold in. Do NOT add curd on direct heat — it will curdle.
Pour raw (unheated) coconut oil on top. Tear curry leaves and scatter over. Do NOT heat the coconut oil — raw coconut oil is the authentic finish.
Serve with rice. Avial thickens as it rests, so make it slightly loose.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Three cardinal rules: (1) Grind the coconut paste COARSE not smooth — avial needs texture. (2) Do NOT add curd while on heat — remove from flame first, let cool slightly, then fold in. (3) Coconut oil must be raw/unheated — pour it directly on top. Also: vegetables should be cooked but firm, not mushy.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Use fewer green chilies (1-2 instead of 4-5) in the coconut paste for kid's portion, or set aside some plain cooked vegetables before adding the coconut paste.

main_dishes.name: Elavan Molagootal (White Pumpkin Molagootal)
main_dishes.description: Palakkad-style molagootal with ash gourd (elavan/white pumpkin) and toor dal, thickened with a coconut-cumin-pepper paste. Mildly spiced, comforting, and protein-rich from the dal.

steps.instruction: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric and enough water until soft (3 whistles). Mash and set aside.
In a pot, cook the ash gourd cubes with salt, a pinch of turmeric, and just enough water to cover. Cook until soft and translucent (10-12 minutes).
Grind coconut (1/2 cup), cumin seeds (1 tsp), black peppercorns (1 tsp), and optional raw rice (1 tsp) to a smooth paste with a little water.
Add the mashed dal to the cooked ash gourd. Mix well.
Add the ground coconut paste. Stir well and simmer on low heat for 7-8 minutes until it thickens to a porridge-like consistency. It should coat the back of a spoon.
Temper: Heat coconut oil in a small pan. Add mustard seeds — when they splutter, add broken dry red chilies and curry leaves. Pour into the molagootal.
Mix gently and serve hot with rice.

main_dishes.critical_notes: The coconut paste should be ground smooth (unlike avial). The molagootal should have a thick, porridge-like consistency — not watery. The pepper gives it a gentle warmth without sharp heat. Palakkad style uses coconut oil for tempering, not ghee.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: This is naturally mild (no chili in the dish, just pepper). Kid-friendly as-is. Just reduce pepper slightly if desired.

main_dishes.name: Keerai Molagootal (Amaranthus Molagootal)
main_dishes.description: Palakkad-style molagootal with amaranthus greens (keerai) and moong dal, thickened with coconut-cumin-pepper paste. Nutritious, iron-rich, and comforting.

steps.instruction: Wash and chop the amaranthus leaves (keerai). Discard thick stems.
Pressure cook moong dal with turmeric until soft (2-3 whistles). Mash and set aside.
In a pot, cook the chopped keerai with 1/4 cup water and salt until wilted and soft (5-7 minutes). The leaves will reduce significantly.
Grind coconut (1/2 cup), cumin seeds (1 tsp), and black peppercorns (1 tsp) to a smooth paste.
Add mashed moong dal to the cooked keerai. Mix well.
Add the ground coconut paste. Stir and simmer on low heat for 5-7 minutes until thickened.
Temper: Heat coconut oil, add mustard seeds, dry red chili, and curry leaves. Pour into the molagootal.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Use moong dal (not toor dal) for keerai molagootal — it cooks faster and has a milder taste that pairs with greens. The dish should be thick, not watery. Keerai reduces a lot when cooked — use generous bunches.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Naturally mild and kid-friendly. The greens are nutritious. If kid resists greens, blend the keerai-dal mixture partially before adding coconut paste.

main_dishes.name: Moru Kootan (Yogurt Curry)
main_dishes.description: Palakkad-style moru kootan — a yogurt-based curry with ash gourd or raw banana, tempered with coconut oil. Cool, tangy, and comforting — perfect for hot days.

steps.instruction: Cook ash gourd cubes in a pot with salt, turmeric, and just enough water to cover until soft and translucent (10-12 minutes).
Grind coconut (1/2 cup), green chilies (2-3), and cumin seeds (1 tsp) to a smooth paste.
Add the ground paste to the cooked vegetable. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Remove from heat. Let it cool for 3-4 minutes — this is important.
Add the whisked curd. Stir gently. Do NOT place back on high heat after adding curd — it will curdle. At most, warm on the lowest flame briefly.
Temper: Heat coconut oil, add mustard seeds, fenugreek seeds, dry red chilies (broken), and curry leaves. Pour over the moru kootan.
Serve warm (not hot) with rice.

main_dishes.critical_notes: CRUCIAL: Do NOT add curd while the curry is on high heat — let it cool first, then add curd and gently warm if needed. Whisking the curd smooth before adding prevents splitting. The consistency should be like a thick soup — not as thick as molagootal.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Use 1 green chili instead of 2-3 for kid's portion. Or set aside some cooked vegetable before adding the coconut-chili paste.

main_dishes.name: Palak Paneer
main_dishes.description: Restaurant-style palak paneer — creamy spinach curry with soft paneer cubes. Rich, vibrant green, and packed with protein.

steps.instruction: Blanch spinach: boil water, add spinach leaves for 2 minutes, then immediately transfer to ice-cold water. This keeps the vibrant green color.
Blend the blanched spinach into a smooth puree. Set aside.
Heat oil/ghee in a pan. Add cumin seeds. When they splutter, add chopped onions and sauté until golden (5-6 minutes).
Add ginger, garlic, and green chilies. Sauté for 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
Add chopped tomatoes. Cook until soft and oil separates (4-5 minutes).
Add coriander powder, red chili powder, and salt. Cook for 1 minute.
Add the spinach puree. Mix well and simmer for 5-7 minutes on low heat.
Add paneer cubes. Gently fold in and simmer for 3-4 minutes. Don't overcook the paneer — it should be soft.
Add cream/butter and garam masala. Stir gently. Simmer 2 more minutes.
Serve hot with roti/naan.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Blanch + ice bath is key for the bright green color. Don't overcook spinach after pureeing — it turns dull. Add paneer at the end so it stays soft. Cream at the end for richness.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Use 1 green chili instead of 2-3. Set aside kid's portion before adding garam masala if kid is sensitive to it. Paneer is kid-friendly and good protein.

main_dishes.name: Mutter Paneer
main_dishes.description: Comforting mutter paneer — green peas and paneer in a creamy onion-tomato gravy with aromatic spices.

steps.instruction: Soak cashews in warm water for 15 minutes. Grind to a smooth paste. Set aside.
Heat oil/ghee. Add cumin seeds. When they splutter, add chopped onions. Sauté until golden brown (7-8 minutes).
Add ginger-garlic paste. Sauté for 2 minutes until raw smell goes.
Add tomato puree, turmeric, red chili powder, coriander powder, and salt. Cook on medium heat until oil separates from the masala (8-10 minutes). This is important for depth of flavor.
Add cashew paste. Mix well and cook for 2-3 minutes.
Add 1 cup water. Bring to a simmer. Add green peas and cook for 5-7 minutes until peas are tender.
Add paneer cubes. Simmer for 3-4 minutes. Don't overcook.
Add cream, garam masala, and crushed kasuri methi. Stir gently. Simmer 2 minutes.
Garnish with coriander leaves. Serve with roti.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Cook the masala until oil separates — this is key for rich flavor. Cashew paste makes it creamy without too much cream. Add paneer late so it stays soft. Kasuri methi at the end adds authentic dhaba-style aroma.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Reduce red chili powder to 1/4 tsp for kid's portion. The peas and paneer are naturally kid-friendly. Cashew cream makes it mild.

main_dishes.name: Veg Kolhapuri
main_dishes.description: Spicy Maharashtrian-style mixed vegetable curry with a complex masala of coconut, sesame seeds, and dried spices. Bold, fiery, and flavorful.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.quantity: 2 cups (potato, cauliflower, beans, carrot, capsicum, peas)

steps.instruction: Make the Kolhapuri masala: Dry roast coconut, sesame seeds, poppy seeds, dry red chilies, coriander seeds, cumin seeds, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon, and fennel seeds in a pan until fragrant (3-4 minutes). Cool and grind to a fine paste.
Boil or steam the mixed vegetables until just tender (not mushy). Drain and set aside.
Heat oil in a heavy pan. Add chopped onions and sauté until deep golden brown (8-10 minutes). Patience here = flavor.
Add ginger-garlic paste. Sauté for 2 minutes.
Add tomato puree, turmeric, and salt. Cook until oil separates (8-10 minutes).
Add the ground Kolhapuri masala paste. Cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring continuously.
Add 1/2 cup water and the cooked vegetables. Simmer for 5-7 minutes until everything melds together.
Garnish with coriander leaves. Serve hot with roti.

main_dishes.critical_notes: The Kolhapuri masala is what makes this dish — roast it properly until fragrant, then grind fine. Onions must be deep golden (not just soft) for the authentic taste. This dish is meant to be spicy — reduce red chilies if needed but don't skip them.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: This is a spicy dish. For kid: set aside some plain boiled vegetables before adding to the Kolhapuri gravy, and serve with mild dal instead.

main_dishes.name: Egg Curry
main_dishes.description: Simple, flavorful egg curry — boiled eggs in a spiced onion-tomato gravy. Great protein, pairs perfectly with roti or rice.

steps.instruction: Hard-boil eggs: Place eggs in water, bring to boil, cook for 10 minutes. Cool in cold water, peel. Make 2-3 shallow slits on each egg so gravy seeps in.
Heat oil. Add cumin seeds. When they splutter, add onions and sauté until golden brown (6-7 minutes).
Add ginger-garlic paste and green chilies. Sauté 2 minutes.
Add tomato puree, turmeric, red chili powder, coriander powder, and salt. Cook until oil separates (7-8 minutes).
Add 1 cup water. Bring to a simmer.
Gently add the boiled eggs. Simmer for 8-10 minutes so the eggs absorb the gravy flavors.
Add garam masala. Garnish with coriander leaves. Serve with roti or rice.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Make slits in the boiled eggs so the gravy penetrates. Cook the masala until oil separates for depth. Let the eggs simmer in the gravy for at least 8 minutes — the longer they sit, the more flavorful they get.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Reduce red chili powder to 1/4 tsp for kid's egg. Or keep one egg aside and serve with just a little mild gravy.

main_dishes.name: Schezwan Egg Fried Rice
main_dishes.description: Spicy Indo-Chinese egg fried rice with schezwan sauce, vegetables, and scrambled eggs. A household favorite for variety days.

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.quantity: to taste (careful — soy sauce is salty)

steps.instruction: Use day-old rice or cook rice and spread on a plate to cool completely. Cold rice = no clumping = better fried rice.
Beat eggs with a pinch of salt. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wok on HIGH heat. Scramble eggs quickly into large pieces. Remove and set aside.
In the same wok, heat 2 tbsp oil on HIGH heat. The wok must be very hot.
Add minced garlic and spring onion whites. Stir-fry for 30 seconds.
Add onions, carrots, and capsicum. Stir-fry on high heat for 2-3 minutes. Vegetables should be crisp, not soggy.
Add schezwan sauce and stir-fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the cold rice. Toss well to coat every grain with the sauce. Stir-fry on high heat for 3-4 minutes.
Add soy sauce, vinegar, green chilies, and white pepper. Toss well.
Add back the scrambled eggs. Toss to combine.
Garnish with spring onion greens. Serve hot.

main_dishes.critical_notes: Three keys: (1) Use cold/day-old rice — warm rice becomes mushy. (2) Wok must be VERY hot throughout — high heat is non-negotiable for fried rice. (3) Don't overcrowd the wok — work in batches if needed. Move fast, keep tossing.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Set aside a portion of plain fried rice (after step 5) before adding schezwan sauce. Add just soy sauce for the kid's portion. Or make kid's portion with less schezwan (1 tsp).

main_dishes.name: Dal Khichdi
main_dishes.description: Comforting one-pot khichdi — rice and moong dal cooked together with mild spices and ghee. Ultimate comfort food, easy to digest, and nutritious.

steps.instruction: Wash rice and moong dal together 2-3 times until water runs clear. Soak for 15 minutes (optional but helps cook faster).
Heat 1 tbsp ghee in a pressure cooker. Add cumin seeds. When they splutter, add hing, green chilies, and grated ginger. Sauté for 1 minute.
Add tomato and vegetables (if using). Sauté for 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice + dal, turmeric, salt, and 3.5 cups water (for a porridge-like consistency) or 3 cups (for a firmer texture).
Pressure cook for 3-4 whistles on medium heat.
Once pressure releases, open and stir gently. Adjust consistency with hot water if too thick.
Top with remaining 1 tbsp ghee (generous!), curry leaves, and coriander leaves.
Serve hot with papad, pickle, and curd.

main_dishes.critical_notes: The ratio of water determines consistency — 3.5 cups for porridge-like (our preference), 3 cups for grainier. Generous ghee on top is essential — don't skip it. This is comfort food; it should be rich.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: Naturally kid-friendly! Mild and easy to digest. Skip green chili for kid's portion. Mash slightly for younger kids.

main_dishes.name: Dhokar Dalna
main_dishes.description: Classic Bengali dish — fried chana dal cakes (dhokar) simmered in a spiced tomato-potato gravy. High in protein, unique in flavor, and a Bengali household staple.

ingredients.name: Oil
ingredients.quantity: for shallow frying + 2 tbsp for gravy

steps.instruction: Soak chana dal for at least 4 hours (or overnight). Drain well.
Grind the soaked dal to a thick, coarse paste (like idli batter consistency) with ginger paste (1/2 tbsp), turmeric (1/4 tsp), salt, and minimal water.

Heat 1 tsp oil in a non-stick pan. Spread the dal paste into a flat cake (1/2 inch thick). Cook on medium-low heat, covered, for 5-6 minutes each side until firm and lightly golden. Let cool, then cut into diamond or square pieces.
Shallow fry the dal cakes (dhokar) in oil until golden and crispy on both sides. Drain on paper towels.
For the gravy: Heat oil + ghee. Add bay leaves, cumin seeds, and dry red chilies.
Add potato cubes. Fry until lightly golden (4-5 minutes). Remove and set aside.
In the same oil, add remaining ginger paste. Sauté for 1 minute. Add tomato puree, turmeric, red chili powder, cumin powder, coriander powder, and salt. Cook until oil separates (6-7 minutes).
Add 1.5 cups water, fried potatoes, and sugar. Simmer until potatoes are cooked (8-10 minutes).
Gently add the fried dhokar pieces. Simmer for 5 minutes so they absorb some gravy. Don't stir too vigorously — dhokar are delicate.
Finish with garam masala and a drizzle of ghee. Serve with rice.

main_dishes.critical_notes: The dal paste must be thick (not runny) or the cakes won't hold. Don't skip the soaking time — at least 4 hours. Be gentle when adding dhokar to gravy — they break easily. The Bengali touch of sugar in the gravy is subtle but important — balances the spice.
main_dishes.kid_adaptation: The dhokar cakes themselves are mild and kid-friendly (essentially fried dal cakes). Serve kid's portion with less gravy or with plain dhokar dipped in mild dal.

side_dishes.name: Beans Poriyal
side_dishes.description: Simple Palakkad-style beans poriyal — French beans stir-fried with coconut, mustard seeds, and curry leaves. Everyday side dish.

steps.instruction: Chop beans finely (small pieces, about 1/4 inch).
Heat coconut oil. Add mustard seeds — when they splutter, add urad dal and fry until golden.
Add broken red chilies and curry leaves. Sauté 10 seconds.
Add chopped beans, turmeric, and salt. Sprinkle 2 tbsp water. Cover and cook on medium-low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until beans are cooked but still have a slight bite.
Add grated coconut. Toss well for 1-2 minutes on low heat. The coconut should coat the beans.
Serve as a side with sambar + rice.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Chop beans fine for even cooking. Cook covered with minimal water — the beans should steam, not boil. Add coconut at the very end so it doesn't burn. Coconut oil is essential for authentic Palakkad taste.

side_dishes.name: Cabbage Poriyal
side_dishes.description: Quick cabbage stir-fry with coconut — South Indian style.

steps.instruction: Finely shred the cabbage. Wash and drain well.
Heat coconut oil. Add mustard seeds, urad dal, red chilies, curry leaves.
Add shredded cabbage, turmeric, and salt. Stir-fry on medium heat for 5-6 minutes. Cabbage cooks fast — should be cooked but still slightly crunchy.
Add grated coconut, toss for 1 minute. Serve.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Don't overcook — cabbage should retain a slight crunch. No water needed; cabbage releases its own moisture.

side_dishes.name: Ivy Gourd Mezhukkuvaratty (Kovakkai)
side_dishes.description: Kerala/Palakkad-style mezhukkuvaratty — ivy gourd (kovakkai) stir-fried in coconut oil with minimal spices. Simple, rustic, and delicious.

steps.instruction: Slice ivy gourd into thin rounds. If seeds are hard, halve and scrape out.
Heat coconut oil. Add mustard seeds, curry leaves.
Add sliced shallots. Sauté until translucent (2-3 minutes).
Add ivy gourd slices, turmeric, red chili powder, and salt. Stir-fry on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the ivy gourd is cooked and slightly crispy at edges.
The key is patience — let it cook without adding water. It should be dry and slightly caramelized.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Do NOT add water. The mezhukkuvaratty should be dry and slightly crispy. Cook on medium heat with patience — stirring occasionally but letting it sit and get some color. Coconut oil is essential.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Reduce red chili powder for kid. Otherwise kid-friendly.

side_dishes.name: Ladies Finger Mezhukkuvaratty (Bhindi/Okra)
side_dishes.description: Okra stir-fried Kerala-style in coconut oil — crispy, non-slimy, and addictive.

steps.instruction: Wash okra and dry completely — this is critical. Any moisture makes it slimy. Pat dry with a towel.
Cut into 1/2 inch rounds or slit lengthwise.
Heat coconut oil. Add mustard seeds and curry leaves.
Add shallots, sauté 2 minutes.
Add okra, turmeric, red chili powder, and salt. Stir-fry on medium-high heat for 10-12 minutes. Do NOT cover — covering creates steam and makes it slimy.
Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until okra is cooked through and slightly crispy.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Two rules for non-slimy okra: (1) Dry the okra completely before cutting. (2) Cook UNCOVERED on medium-high heat — never cover the pan. No water!
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Reduce chili powder. Otherwise kid-friendly — many kids like crispy okra.

side_dishes.name: Yardlong Beans Mezhukkuvaratty (Payar)
side_dishes.description: Yard-long beans (payar) stir-fried Kerala-style. Similar technique to other mezhukkuvaratties.

steps.instruction: Cut yardlong beans into small pieces (1/2 inch).
Heat coconut oil. Temper with mustard seeds, curry leaves.
Add shallots, sauté until translucent.
Add beans, turmeric, red chili powder, salt. Sprinkle 2 tbsp water. Cover and cook on medium-low heat for 10-12 minutes until tender.
Uncover, add grated coconut, toss for 1-2 minutes. Serve.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Unlike okra, yardlong beans need a little water and covering to cook through. But final step should be uncovered to evaporate any moisture.

side_dishes.name: Olan
side_dishes.description: Classic Kerala olan — ash gourd and cowpeas simmered in thin coconut milk, finished with coconut oil and curry leaves. Subtle, elegant, and a Sadya essential.

ingredients.name: Cowpeas (black-eyed peas / karamani)
ingredients.quantity: 1/4 cup, soaked overnight or use canned

steps.instruction: If using dried cowpeas, soak overnight and pressure cook until tender. Drain.
In a heavy-bottomed pan, cook ash gourd cubes with thin coconut milk, slit green chilies, and salt. Simmer on medium heat until ash gourd is soft and translucent (12-15 minutes).
Add the cooked cowpeas. Simmer for 3-4 minutes.
Add thick coconut milk. Stir gently. Let it just come to a gentle simmer — do NOT boil vigorously after adding thick coconut milk.
Remove from heat. Pour raw coconut oil on top. Add curry leaves.
Let rest for 10 minutes before serving — olan develops flavor as it rests.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Olan is a subtle dish — don't overpower with spices. The only 'spice' is green chili. Do NOT boil after adding thick coconut milk. Raw coconut oil at the end is essential for the characteristic flavor. This should taste gentle and coconutty.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Use 1-2 green chilies instead of 3-4. Otherwise naturally mild and kid-friendly.

side_dishes.name: Thayir Pachadi (Yogurt Raita)
side_dishes.description: South Indian yogurt raita — vegetables in seasoned yogurt with a coconut oil tempering. Cool and tangy side dish.

steps.instruction: If using cucumber: finely dice and add to whisked curd with salt. If using ladies finger: sauté chopped okra in a little oil until cooked and slightly crispy, then cool and add to curd.
Optional: Grind coconut (2 tbsp) + green chili into a coarse paste. Mix into the curd.
Temper: Heat coconut oil, add mustard seeds, dry red chili, curry leaves. Pour over the pachadi.
Mix gently. Serve cold/room temperature as a side.

side_dishes.critical_notes: If using okra for thayir pachadi, the okra must be fully cooled before adding to curd. The curd should be fresh and not too sour.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Skip green chili. Naturally mild and cooling — great for kids.

side_dishes.name: Puli Pachadi (Ladies Finger)
side_dishes.description: Tangy-sweet-spicy pachadi with fried okra in a tamarind-jaggery-coconut sauce. A Palakkad specialty.

steps.instruction: Deep/shallow fry the okra rounds in coconut oil until crispy. Drain and set aside.
Soak tamarind in 1/2 cup warm water. Extract juice.
Grind coconut into a coarse paste.
In a pan, combine tamarind extract, red chili powder, turmeric, jaggery, and salt. Cook on medium heat until it thickens (5-7 minutes).
Add the coconut paste. Stir and cook 2-3 minutes.
Add the fried okra. Mix gently.
Temper with mustard seeds, dry red chilies, and curry leaves in coconut oil. Pour over.

side_dishes.critical_notes: The balance of tamarind (sour) + jaggery (sweet) + chili (heat) is the magic of puli pachadi. Adjust to taste. Okra must be crispy when added — it will soften slightly in the sauce.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: This is tangy-spicy. For kid: serve a small amount or skip for very young kids.

side_dishes.name: Thogayal (Coconut Chutney — Thick)
side_dishes.description: Thick, concentrated chutney/thogayal — ground coconut with roasted dal, chilies, and tamarind. Eaten in small amounts mixed with rice.

steps.instruction: Heat 1 tsp oil. Roast urad dal and chana dal until golden. Add dry red chilies and asafoetida. Roast for 30 seconds. Cool.
Grind the roasted mixture with coconut, tamarind, salt, and very little water into a thick, coarse paste. It should NOT be a smooth chutney — thogayal is thick and textured.
Serve a small dollop with rice and ghee. Mix into hot rice.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Thogayal is thick — not a pourable chutney. Use minimal water when grinding. It's concentrated — a small amount goes a long way. Best eaten mixed into hot rice with a drop of ghee.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Reduce red chilies to 1-2 for a milder version.

side_dishes.name: Tofu Stir-Fry
side_dishes.description: Quick protein-packed tofu stir-fry with soy sauce, garlic, and vegetables. Great as a side with fried rice.

steps.instruction: Press tofu to remove excess water. Cut into cubes. Toss with cornstarch and a pinch of salt.
Heat oil in a pan on high heat. Fry tofu cubes until golden and crispy on all sides (5-6 minutes). Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add a little more oil. Sauté garlic for 30 seconds.
Add onion and capsicum. Stir-fry on high heat for 2 minutes.
Add soy sauce, chili sauce, and vinegar. Toss.
Add back the crispy tofu. Toss to coat with the sauce.
Garnish with spring onions and sesame seeds. Serve hot.

side_dishes.critical_notes: Press tofu well — dry tofu = crispy tofu. Cornstarch coating is key for crispiness. High heat throughout.
side_dishes.kid_adaptation: Skip chili sauce/flakes for kid's portion. Soy sauce flavor alone is usually kid-friendly.
